Loss of engine power with zero oil pressure and temperature indications points to an engine-level failure, likely internal engine malfunction or oil loss.
Oil pressure and oil temperature gauges reading zero suggests loss of engine oil or oil system failure as a mechanism for the power loss.
The forced landing onto a road with cars and a guardrail impact indicates the surface and roadway environment contributed to the accident outcome.

Maintenance was deferred and records were inaccurate: the logbook claimed ELT removal and AD checks that did not occur, the ADs were signed by an apprentice, and the oil filter was not changed, indicating deficient maintenance and record keeping.

The FAA inspector issued the Special Flight Permit without a physical inspection or itemized AD review, and the agency lacked procedures for Part 91 special flight permits, indicating deficient regulatory oversight.

Postaccident teardown of the right engine showed blocked fuel injectors, corrosion, and debris, and witnesses reported it was hard to start and would not produce full power, supporting an engine power-loss contributor; however the left engine and propellers also showed issues and the causal weighting is uncertain.
Fuel leaking from the inboard and auxiliary tanks during fueling and the pilot needing to transfer fuel in flight point to a fuel system deficiency, though fuel exhaustion is not established.
The absence of FAA policy or procedures for issuing special flight permits via the AWC tool, and reliance on local practice, reflects a policy/procedure deficiency at the organizational level.
Left wing separated from fuselage after a bang and hard left turn with the left wing dipping into water, suggesting a wing structural failure or attachment failure as a primary mechanism.
Bang and cable-snap sounds with a hard left roll and flap attachment arm bent suggest a possible flight control or cable/linkage failure, though continuity was confirmed and the cause is unresolved.
Key evidence such as floats and fly wires was unrecovered and the wind and cause remain undetermined, so the cause may not be determinable from the packet.

Engine No. 2 compressor section showed rotor imbalance, rub damage, and out-of-tolerance clearances, indicating a turboshaft engine internal malfunction leading to the power loss and speed/torque mismatch.

The compressor bleed valve diaphragm hole and the valve hanging up during transition affected engine fuel/governing balance, contributing to the engine synchronization difficulties and torque mismatch.

Maintenance personnel continued operating the engine after a new compressor was installed and the loud howling and synchronization problems were not properly resolved, with a near-life-limited bleed valve left in place.

The pilot decided to continue flying with unresolved engine synchronization issues, an abnormal howling sound, and an approaching overhaul bleed valve, reflecting poor information processing and decision making.

The pilot's response to the power imbalance, including trim adjustments and maneuvering near trees and power lines during a low-altitude climb, reflects control parameter management problems leading to the descent into trees.

Flat light conditions over featureless tundra and diffuse sky with low stratiform clouds and haze likely limited visual perception of altitude, a visibility/light condition hazard central to this controlled flight into terrain accident.

The pilot likely misjudged altitude and attitude over featureless, flat-light terrain, consistent with perception/orientation illusion and the flight at about 144 ft msl at 93 knots described as too fast for the conditions.
The pilot chose to operate low and fast in marginal visual conditions over flat terrain contrary to SOP minimums and DNR altitude restrictions, reflecting an information processing or decision error.
The operator failed to ensure the pilot received the DNR permit altitude restrictions and flat-light procedures, indicating a training and oversight deficiency.
The operator lacked a flight operational quality assurance program and did not review flight data, and the overdue alert went unnoticed, pointing to weak safety program monitoring.

The propeller pitch control nut lacked a cotter pin and showed mechanical damage, and the propeller system (pitch control and blade components) is the likely failure point behind the rpm loss and inability to maintain altitude.
The propeller overhaul records are incomplete and the pitch control nut was found without its cotter pin, pointing to a maintenance or overhaul task that was not properly completed or documented.
Missing cotter pin and unsecured castellated nut on the pitch control bolt suggest improper maintenance task performance during the propeller overhaul.
Pitch control linkage and blade pitch change components were damaged and spalled, which affects rotorcraft-style propeller pitch control and could contribute to the power loss and rpm fluctuations.
The precise sequence linking the pitch control nut damage to the rpm drop cannot be fully established from the packet alone, so the cause remains partially undetermined.

The pilot apparently mismanaged fuel, with the left tank empty and the right tank still holding about 25 gallons, indicating an info processing or fuel management decision error leading to fuel exhaustion.
Improper use of the fuel selector or fuel quantity information led to the loss of engine power, consistent with fuel exhaustion on a tank that was not properly monitored.
The fuel system was involved because the engine lost power while fuel selection and the fuel system were the relevant pathway, although no system malfunction was found.

The pilot descended toward power lines at night in a seemingly level flight pattern, suggesting a poor information processing or decision-making error such as failure to maintain altitude awareness or misjudging clearance from obstacles.

Night conditions with a landing light and a brief loss of visibility during the descent suggest possible perception or orientation difficulties, including spatial disorientation or obstacle-perception illusions, though this is not confirmed by the packet.

The student pilot had only about 120 total hours with 10 hours in the prior six months and no available logbooks, which suggests limited experience for an unplanned night flight in the traffic pattern near power lines.
The cause cannot be definitively determined from the packet because the wreckage showed no flight control malfunction and the engine's fuel and carburetor conditions remain uncertain.

The pilot was moving belongings to a new hangar before taking off for extra laps, suggesting possible task saturation or divided attention that may have contributed to the loss of situational awareness.
Tailwind and gusty wind conditions caused the airspeed to drop below effective translational lift, a wind-related environmental factor central to this accident.
The pilot continued the low-altitude descent near terrain and power lines in gusty conditions he had said he avoided, reflecting a poor information processing or decision in flight.
Operating near maximum gross weight at low altitude in a confined area with obstacles increased the demands on the pilot's workload management during the descent.
Power transmission lines and trees constrained the available space and prevented a turn into the wind, making the obstacles a physical environment contributor.

Loss of engine power after a fuel-related sequence, with a fuel selector detent anomaly, fuel pump replacement and a recorded fuel system adjustment, points to a fuel system malfunction as the mechanism.
Engine fuel and control issues are implicated by the reported loss of engine power and the fuel pressure adjustment, with the engine test run noting the fuel pressure and mixture relationship.
The fuel system adjustment and fuel pump overhaul performed about 18 months before the flight may reflect a maintenance task performance deficiency, though records are not conclusive.
The pilot had owned the airplane only about one month and had limited familiarization, which may have contributed to fuel management issues, though this is speculative.
The fuel control unit (FCU) housing fatigue fracture and missing bolt, with a reactive gap movement, point to a failure within the engine fuel and control system causing the power loss.
The turboprop engine experienced a loss of power requiring manufacturer examination, indicating an engine (turbine) component failure as the proximate mechanism.
Records show time-since-new and airframe/engine time discrepancies and a TBO exceedance relative to the manufacturer's recommendation, suggesting possible maintenance or records-related deficiencies.
Mismatched engine TSN (14,217 vs 14,092 hours) and airplane TSN (12,475 hours) entries in logbooks indicate record-keeping inconsistencies.
The missing bolt on the FCU housing is a misc hardware fastener issue that may have allowed the housing separation leading to the fracture.
Cracks in the fuselage/tail boom skin with disbonded splice straps indicate a structural failure of the fuselage skin, which the packet documents as the damaged component.
The damaged tail boom structure adjacent to the vertical stabilizer suggests empennage structural involvement, though the failure is primarily in the boom skin.
The pilot's final glide at 79 kts and the vibration encountered near 60 kts relate to operating within the airspeed envelope, a possible performance/control parameter factor.
No runway or surface factor is indicated in the packet; included only as a low-confidence placeholder, so it is probably not applicable.
The long line wrapped around the main rotor mast during external load operations, indicating a performance/control parameter issue in the external load task rather than a mechanical failure.
The pilot's decision to continue external load operations with a long line and a known oil leak, under catch-up pressure, reflects info processing or decision issues leading to the rotor strike.
The afternoon schedule was a catch-up day resulting from maintenance delays, which increased workload and pressure during external load drops.
The long line was not released before the rotor strike, suggesting improper use of the emergency cargo release or cargo hook equipment during the external load task.
Loss of power with no compression on cylinder No. 4 and a stuck exhaust valve points to an engine internal (valve/power plant) malfunction as the source of the power loss.
The sustained power loss with the engine remaining at 1,000 rpm and a failed troubleshooting attempt indicates a general power plant malfunction, with the specific mechanism not fully determined.

Maintenance performed a week before the accident (pushrod seal replacement and new left magneto installation) may have been a contributing factor to the engine failure, though the link is unconfirmed.
The exact cause of the valve sticking and compression loss could not be determined from the post-accident examination, so the cause remains undetermined.
Pilot and passenger failed to properly use fuel system information and management, leading to fuel exhaustion with the center header tank empty and mains depleted despite estimated fuel on board.
The fuel system was involved: a fuel cap installed backwards with the vent facing the trailing edge disrupted fuel flow from the auxiliary tank, and the fuel system was found empty.
The line technician improperly installed the vented fuel cap after fueling, a maintenance/servicing task performance error.
Weather was VMC with light winds and no meteorological contribution was indicated.

The pilot turned the airplane 150° shortly after a short-field climb-out and during the turn the airplane lost climb performance and stalled or lost control, suggesting an inadequate decision or information-processing response to the performance loss, such as maneuvering with insufficient airspeed.

The airplane was flown in a turn at low altitude after takeoff with a nose-high attitude and decreased performance, pointing to a performance/control parameter issue such as exceeding a safe climb or turn airspeed margin.
The narrative notes atmospheric conditions conducive to icing at glide power per the icing probability chart, which may have contributed to the loss of performance.

The pilot's experience and qualifications in a high-performance taildragger or homebuilt type are not documented, and an inadequate-experience factor could contribute to mishandling a performance loss after takeoff.
The airplane struck power lines during low-altitude agricultural operations near terrain and obstacles, so the terrain/obstacle environment is a contributing physical factor.
The pilot flew a clean-up pass near structures and then turned back toward the field, suggesting an information processing or decision error in judging the obstacle lines during a low-level maneuver.
Power lines along the south side of the road are hard to perceive during low-level agricultural flight, so a perception or obstacle-recognition lapse is plausible.
The flight began before dawn-to-morning hours and involved repetitive low-level passes, so fatigue is possible but the record contains no direct evidence of it.

The pilot apparently chose a steep low-altitude departure with full flaps and gear down, which in a 45-second flight suggests an information processing or decision error regarding configuration and climb performance.
The pilot departed on a test flight after a propeller and interior change without a documented performance check, indicating inadequate flight planning or preparation for the takeoff configuration.
The POM did not address takeoff with full flaps, suggesting the pilot may have lacked knowledge or training on the airplane's configuration limits after the new propeller installation.

The flap handle was found fully extended, and the steep left bank with the landing gear down suggests a configuration-related loss of control rather than a flight control malfunction, so this is a low-confidence finding.
The airport manager reported the pilot was frustrated about delays, which may have contributed to a hurried decision to fly without adequate preparation.
Engine lost fuel pressure and power on final after the pilot likely ran a tank dry with uneven fuel distribution, pointing to a fuel system/fuel supply issue.
Pilot allowed fuel to run low and flew sightseeing flights with imbalanced tanks and low total fuel, indicating a fuel-management decision/information processing error.
Pre-flight and in-flight fuel planning was inadequate given only about 15 gallons remained with unequal tank quantities before two additional flights.
Improper use of the fuel selector and tank quantity information, with the pilot operating on Both with an unbalanced, low fuel state, relates to use of equipment/information.
The experimental GM LS-3 reciprocating engine's PCV valve failed, indicating an engine-level malfunction as the likely origin of the forced landing and damage.
The packet states the PCV valve failed for undetermined reasons, so the underlying cause of the failure is not established.
The PCV valve is part of the crankcase ventilation and oil system, so its failure may have affected engine oil system operation.

The pilot slowed in turns at 1.8 g load factor with airspeed near 87 mph, below the accelerated stall speed of about 89 mph, indicating an inadvertent aerodynamic stall and spin resulting from poor information processing or decision making during maneuvering.

The pilot had only 33 hours in the AT-6D with a single 1.0-hour checkout flight lacking documented maneuvers, suggesting limited type-specific experience relevant to handling the aircraft at low speed and high load factor.
Winds were light at 4 kt, so wind is unlikely to be a causal factor, and including it would be weak support.

The pilot flew low-altitude agricultural spray passes at about 34 ft agl near powerlines and did not perceive or avoid the wires, indicating a decision/information-processing failure regarding obstacle awareness.
Powerlines were a significant object hazard in the operating area, and the middle wires severed in the collision, so the object/obstacle environment contributed to the accident.
Repeated east-west passes near the wires suggest the pilot's attention to the obstacle was insufficient during spraying, consistent with an attention/monitoring lapse.
Agricultural spraying at low altitude with a cluster of fields and turns may have created a high workload that contributed to missing the wires.

The airplane was airborne about 3 hours 37 minutes on roughly 34 usable gallons with an endurance of 3.9 to 4.0 hours, indicating the pilot likely failed to properly assess fuel quantity and endurance during flight planning and in-flight decisions, leading to fuel exhaustion.
The flight likely involved inadequate preflight planning of fuel requirements and reserves given the endurance margin, which is a planning/preparation deficiency.
The fuel system is implicated because no usable fuel remained in the tanks, though the tanks were intact and no fuel system malfunction was found, so this is a weaker fit than fuel management.

The pilot continued a low-and-slow turn back toward the airport after a loud pop and wing drop, suggesting a poor information-processing or decision choice at low altitude during a maneuver that the airplane could not sustain.
The cause of the loud pop and wing drop could not be determined because the wreckage was largely consumed by fire and no preimpact anomalies were found.
The pilot departed on a long cross-country with known unresolved overheating and performance problems and a planned fly-by, indicating questionable flight planning and preparation.
The low and slow turn near terrain and the rotating nose-low descent point to a performance or control-parameter exceedance during the maneuver.

Nose-high attitude during initial climb followed by left wing drop and nosedive suggests a possible aerodynamic stall or loss of control from a poor decision or information processing error during takeoff.
The pilot had only about 175 total hours with limited recent experience, which may have contributed to inadequate handling of a low-altitude upset after takeoff.
Abrupt nose-high climb and left wing drop at low altitude point to a performance/control parameter exceedance such as stall or insufficient airspeed during climb.
Spatial disorientation at night-dawn light conditions during takeoff could explain a nose-high attitude and wing drop, though the evidence is weak.
The first officer (pilot flying) applied large nose-down and nose-up control column inputs after main gear touchdown, a pilot action that caused the nosewheel bounces and high nose gear sink rates.

The flight crew did not correctly use the speedbrake and landing technique per the Flight Training Manual, with speedbrakes deploying during the bounce and the control column being mishandled during the landing roll.
The first officer had unsatisfactory checkride performance including landings and was on a short cycle, indicating reduced landing proficiency that may have contributed to the control inputs.
The airframe structural damage to the fuselage crown was caused by high vertical loads from the de-rotation, though the flight control system itself was not a causal factor.

Departing a high-density-altitude airport (about 6,607 ft density altitude) with full fuel and passengers and a gross weight of 2,500 lbs likely exceeded the airplane's climb capability, a workload/planning demand on the pilot's takeoff decision.

The pilot's decision to continue a takeoff that failed to climb as expected, followed by a shallow turn and a landing in an open field with rising terrain ahead, reflects poor information processing and decision-making under time pressure.
The airplane's climb performance was insufficient for the high-density-altitude, heavy-gross-weight takeoff, indicating a performance/control parameter mismatch.
The pilot's experience and understanding of performance limits at high density altitude with a heavy load appear to have been inadequate, given the failure to anticipate reduced climb performance.
Takeoff planning appears not to have accounted for density altitude, full fuel and passenger load, and the rising terrain beyond the runway departure end.
The gyroplane pilot performed a 360° left turn and a hard turn on base leg despite briefings not to do so for spacing, which is an action-level error in the traffic pattern.
The helicopter occupants apparently did not detect or avoid the gyroplane in the traffic pattern before impact, consistent with an attention/monitoring lapse in see-and-avoid.
Pilots were repeatedly asked to communicate intentions in the pattern, and the gyroplane's unexpected maneuvers were not communicated, suggesting a personnel communication shortfall.
The FFZ operation relied on verbal briefings and air-boss discretion for pattern changes rather than enforced procedures, which contributed to mixed traffic flows at the same time.
The calculated crosswind of about 10 kt and tailwind of about 6 kt on a taxiway heading contributed to the weathervaning tendency that initiated the left veer and ground loop.
The pilot's delayed or inadequate response to the developing left veer during taxi, with crosswind and tailwind conditions, suggests a decision/information-processing issue in correcting the turn.

The taildragger's directional control performance during taxi with differential braking was insufficient to counter the turning moment, pointing to the aircraft control parameters exceeded in the conditions.
The taxiway surface departure into grass and the tire marks indicate the surface condition at the taxiway edge may have influenced directional control.
Fractured and stripped left main landing gear mounting studs with missing attachment nut point to a landing gear system failure that led to the wheel locking up and the ground loop.
Buckling of the right wing, fuselage and main landing gear mount structure plus fractured left main gear mounting studs indicate a structural failure of the airframe/gear attachment area.
The pilot's conflicting post-accident accounts of a ground loop, locked wheel, or stuck brake suggest possible difficulty managing the directional control response during the landing roll.
The pilot had no recent night flight experience and landed at dusk, which may have contributed to difficulty controlling the airplane during the landing roll.

Progressive engine power decline followed by total power loss with idle mixture found nearly full-lean points to an engine fuel and control problem, though fuel and servo were otherwise found unremarkable.

The pilot did not attempt an engine restart or run the emergency checklist, and applied full throttle and abrupt stick inputs near the ground, which may reflect inappropriate action during the power loss.
The specific cause of the power loss could not be determined because the electronic ignition system could not be tested and no definitive failure was found in the fuel, engine, or oil systems.

The pilot misjudged fuel remaining and did not act on the early fuel imbalance warning (tank levels and fuel odor), instead balancing tanks and continuing, leading to fuel exhaustion in flight; this reflects information processing and decision error.

The pilot's use of the fuel selector and fuel quantity indications was inadequate, as he switched selectors without resolving the apparent fuel loss and ran a tank dry, indicating misuse of equipment and information.
The fuel system showed evidence of fuel leakage from the left wing filler port, and fuel loss from the system led to engine power loss, so a fuel system fault is implicated.

The pilot's knowledge of fuel consumption and fuel system behavior appears limited, as he calculated endurance inaccurately and was unfamiliar with the imbalance, though this is weakly supported by the packet.

The pilot had significant coronary artery disease (90% LAD and 75% RCA narrowing), which could have caused incapacitation or impaired performance during flight, although the autopsy did not establish sudden incapacitation.
The helicopter made repeated low-altitude spray passes and a turn over powerlines before impact, suggesting possible inattention to wires or terrain during the maneuvering near the field edge.
The packet does not establish a definitive cause; no preimpact airframe or engine anomaly was found and the wire strike evidence was absent, so the cause remains undetermined.
Blunt force fatal injuries with an uncontrolled impact after a turn and a possible cardiac event leave incapacitation as a possible but unconfirmed contributor.
Cetirizine, which can cause drowsiness and impaired psychomotor performance, was detected, so pilot alertness may have been reduced.

The pilot initiated a go-around and continued climbing with a steep pitch attitude (about 21°) at very low airspeed (about 53 knots), suggesting a poor decision to attempt to out-climb terrain in mountainous, forested surroundings rather than a safe escape path.
The airplane impacted heavily forested, mountainous terrain during the climb after the go-around, indicating that the terrain itself was a hazard to the climbing airplane.
Diphenhydramine, a sedating antihistamine with cognitive and psychomotor slowing effects, was detected in the pilot, which may have impaired his judgment or control inputs during the go-around.
The FAA Safety Team mountain flying guidance on pre-descent planning and go-around options suggests the pilot may not have adequately planned an escape route for a mountain airport approach.
The mountain airport's design and surrounding terrain constrained go-around and departure options, a contributing environmental factor in this accident.

The electrical system failed: the main battery negative terminal fractured with arcing and the main battery read 3.67 V, causing the loss of electrical power to the ignition/instruments and the engine power loss.
The engine lost power and ran rough as the ignition system (plasma CDI boxes powered by the main/aux batteries) was starved of voltage, pointing to an ignition-system power interruption.
The pilot did not switch to the auxiliary battery via IGN A/IGN B or respond to the low voltage indications and dark instruments, which may have contributed to the loss of control.

Maintenance and inspection of the battery terminal connections was apparently inadequate, as the negative terminal was fractured and arcing, suggesting a deficient installation or inspection of the battery hardware.
Contaminated, degraded fuel with gum deposits and particulates in the fuel system points to a fuel system malfunction affecting engine operation.
The pilot failed to filter fuel from the hose before transferring it into the helicopter, a planning/preparation lapse that introduced contamination.
Possible lack of fuel handling guidance or training on contamination, though the packet does not establish this directly.

Tail rotor control failure: pilot had no left pedal response and the tail rotor pitch change lever assembly was found disconnected from the trunnion with a missing bolt and loose nut, pointing to a tail rotor component failure.
Missing bolt, loose nut and missing cotter pin on the pitch change lever assembly indicate a maintenance or inspection lapse in securing the tail rotor linkage.

The fastener deficiencies (missing cotter pin, loose nut, missing bolt) suggest improper maintenance task performance on the tail rotor linkage, though the responsible party is not established in the packet.
Right engine lost power with valve clearances out of spec, exhaust valves not seating, and sparse engine-related evidence, pointing to engine malfunction in the right powerplant.
Maintenance just completed before flight left valve clearances out of specification, exhaust valves unseated, and ignition connections loose, indicating inadequate maintenance and inspection.
Task performance deficiencies during maintenance (valve clearance, loose ignition coil bolts and lead connections, loose crimps) reflect improper maintenance by the builder/repair personnel.
Loose ignition coil and spark plug lead connections and severed ECU injector and power wires indicate engine control and ignition integrity problems on the right engine.
The pilot-builder completed flight testing without single-engine testing guidance, reflecting a training/knowledge gap in experimental aircraft flight test procedures.
Carburetor pistons/diaphragms were misassembled and misaligned, causing rough running and reduced engine performance, which is an engine fuel and control system defect.

Maintenance performed on the carburetors (float replacement and reassembly) led to incorrect assembly of the carburetor piston and diaphragm contrary to the Rotax maintenance manual, a task performance error.

The instructor's decision to continue a low-altitude, steep-turn maneuver with a deteriorating engine and EGT problem, rather than landing straight ahead, reflects poor information processing and decision-making.
The aggressive steep left bank at low altitude after an engine power problem suggests a possible mental or emotional state issue such as startle or stress affecting the pilots' response.
Light surface wind of 8 kt was reported, which is unlikely to be a significant causal factor in this accident.
The left tank fuel vent check valve was blocked by insect debris, preventing air from entering the tank and causing fuel starvation and engine power loss, which is a fuel system failure.
The pilot did not engage the auxiliary fuel pump during restart attempts, an action omission contrary to the air start checklist that could have restored fuel flow.
The pilot misinterpreted the fuel system failure and reported a broken fuel pump shaft, indicating possible misuse or misunderstanding of available equipment and information during the emergency.
Pre-flight inspection of the fuel vent system and check valve for obstructions may have been inadequate, though the packet does not establish this directly.
The packet does not identify the cause; the engine ran normally, flight controls were continuous, and no mechanical failure was documented, so the cause is undetermined.

The airplane departed the runway environment and ended up inverted in trees, suggesting an info processing or decision error during takeoff or low-level maneuvering, though the cause is not established in the packet.

The pilot performed an engine runup and preflight at the runway end, so planning or preparation for the departure is a possible contributing area, but the packet gives no direct evidence of a planning deficiency.
The accident occurred near the runway 18 end and the airplane was displaced laterally into the tree line, so the runway surface or area layout may have been a factor in the departure path.

The pilot's fatal sudden medical event (family heart disease history, awareness of heart attack risk, unresponsive radio, witness heard throttle held, aircraft tracked off runway) suggests incapacitation as a plausible cause.
The airplane took off-runway tracking left with full power and no evident attempt to correct, consistent with a loss of directional control during takeoff roll by the pilot.
Documented heart disease history and a lapsed medical certificate with a deferred cardiac-related medical history suggest a health condition as a contributing factor.
Workload or task management during the takeoff roll is possible but the evidence for it is weak.
The instructor's decision to attempt a steep, high-pitch climb and left turn at low altitude after a short takeoff roll indicates an information processing or decision error during the departure.
The sharp pitch-up and subsequent loss of control in the initial climb suggest improper use of flight controls (elevator/pitch and bank management) by the pilot.
The packet documents a fluctuating wind with a right crosswind component during takeoff, which may have contributed to the handling difficulty in the initial climb.
The flight instructor's experience and qualifications are not documented, so this is only a weak possibility given the handling of the departure.
Engine power loss after takeoff due to cylinder scoring from an out-of-temperature seizure points to an engine (two-stroke) mechanical/power plant failure.
The power plant as a whole experienced the in-flight power loss, with the cylinder seizure as the failure mode in the power plant system.
Overheating-related seizure in a liquid-cooled two-stroke engine may relate to engine cooling and lubrication, though the coolant system itself showed no anomalies.

Radiator louvers were found near fully closed, reducing cooling airflow and likely contributing to overheating, suggesting a pilot information processing or decision error in managing engine temperature.
Improper use of the radiator louver control (left nearly closed) reflects a task performance error in the use of equipment during operation.
Fuel exhaustion/fuel starvation caused the engine to stop, with the fuel sight tube empty and the fuel drain valve leaking, pointing to a fuel system (engine fuel and control) failure.
The fuel system itself failed, as shown by the leaking fuel drain valve with a debris-fouled O-ring seal that allowed fuel loss from the tank.
The pilot misjudged fuel quantity and did not use fuel gauge and tank information properly, believing the tanks were full and rationalizing the discrepancy.
Maintenance of the fuel drain valve was inadequate, as a debris-fouled O-ring allowed a leak that was not caught during preflight sampling.

The pilot performed an aerobatic maneuver (pitch up near vertical, aileron roll, spin) at low altitude over a traffic pattern below 1,500 ft, which reflects a poor risk decision about the maneuver rather than a mechanical failure.
Autopsy toxicology showed HbA1c of 12% and urine glucose of 803 mg/dL, indicating severely uncontrolled diabetes that could impair the pilot's health and fitness to fly.
The pilot's logbook was not recovered and he reported no civil flight hours in 2017, so his experience for low-level formation aerobatics in this setting is questionable.
The pilot was flying a formation honor flight with a ceremony-driven schedule and a second flight after a short break, which may have increased workload and pressure.
Runway and surface conditions are not indicated as contributing; this is a weak association included only to note the low-altitude pattern environment.
Broken power turbine blades, shroud, and bearing failure with high-energy containment rings indicate a turbine engine internal failure as the primary mechanical event.

Improper assembly of the RGB second-stage ring gear and non-PWC tooling marks on the propeller shaft retaining nut point to maintenance/inspection deficiencies, and a non-approved PT vane repair suggests maintenance quality issues.
The ring gear was not assembled per PWC technical publications and the nut/key washer show non-dedicated tool marks, indicating a maintenance task performance error.

The Skycrane crew failed to correctly track the Bell's position and the airspace/NOCOM clearance procedures, indicating an information processing and decision error in conflict awareness before the collision.

Firefighting operations under time pressure and dispatch demands, with the Skycrane crew rushing to reach the incident and multiple competing communications, suggest pressures/demands contributed to the mid-air collision.

Communication breakdowns occurred between the Skycrane crew and ATGS over clearance into the FTA and the Bell's position and intentions, with the Skycrane calling in at an incorrect distance and failing to get clearance.

The FTA and air traffic coordination procedures for deconflicting helicopters within the firefighting airspace were not effectively applied, allowing two helicopters to converge over the same terrain.
Attention and monitoring failures are implied by the Skycrane continuing its descent and turn while the Bell was in level flight nearby and by the lack of visual separation, leading to collision.

The narrative stresses NVG-related distance estimation and depth perception limits and the lack of training on terrain interpretation, suggesting the pilot misperceived the landing zone's distance or terrain during the descent at night.
The approach was made at night under a low-angle moon with NVG use and searchlight, so the light conditions and shadows strongly shaped the visual cues available for the landing zone.
The operator's NVG training program omitted shadows, terrain density, and vegetation, and was only updated after the accident, indicating a training deficiency relevant to the crew's preparation.

The pilot continued the descent toward the road at night with limited terrain interpretation, which could reflect an information-processing or decision error in assessing obstacles and the landing site.
The remote landing zone's terrain and vegetation characteristics, which the NVG-based crew had difficulty interpreting, likely contributed to the hazard the crew encountered during landing.
The packet does not establish the cause of the accident; the wind and visibility are unknown and the fuel and engine findings are inconclusive.
Fuel exhaustion or fuel mismanagement is plausible given no fuel found in tanks or carburetor bowl, suggesting pilot decision/information processing about fuel planning on a long relocation flight.
The pilot's limited familiarity with a newly purchased airplane and a long cross-country relocation suggests possible inadequate flight planning or preparation, including fuel planning.
The accident occurred near McDermitt, Oregon, where the landing surface may have contributed to the forward fuselage crush, though the packet provides no surface details.
The packet gives no cause for the power loss and the wreckage and engine were disposed of, so the cause may remain undetermined.

Loss of altitude and airspeed while the engine kept running in a low-performance experimental airplane points to an engine fuel or power-delivery problem such as fuel starvation or carburetor issues, but no cause was determined.

The pilot maneuvered around clouds and flew toward an airport with declining airspeed and altitude, suggesting an information-processing or decision issue about fuel or route planning, though the narrative does not establish it.
The annual inspection history shows an approximately 11-year gap before the October 2022 inspection, suggesting possible maintenance or record-keeping shortcomings relevant to the accident.
Engine examined with no mechanical anomalies, so an engine malfunction is only weakly suggested; the aircraft was flown with a long maintenance gap, leaving a power plant cause possible but unproven.
Pilot decision-making during the dusk local flight from a grass airstrip may have contributed, though the packet gives no direct evidence of the pilot's choices.

Atmospheric conditions at the time were conducive to serious icing at glide power per the icing chart, and the low-altitude aerial application may have been affected by temperature and humidity conditions.

Low-altitude aerial application at about 68 ft agl with a heavily loaded airplane and a soft-field landing suggests a pilot information processing or decision issue, though the evidence is not conclusive.
The airplane landed on a soft field and nosed over, indicating the runway/land surface contributed to the accident.
Engine was separated and some cylinders showed dirt and debris, but the engine examination did not establish a powerplant malfunction as cause.
The airplane was loaded with substantial pesticide and fuel for the flight, suggesting possible workload or load management pressures during the application task.
Crankshaft rear gear and its attaching bolts and dowel pin failed, stopping accessory drive and producing low or no power, indicating an engine power plant failure.
The failure involved the rear crankshaft accessory drive gear that drives the accessory case, so the accessory gear is a direct locus of the finding.
The pilot had only 2.8 hours in the Cessna 150 and recently obtained FAA certification, suggesting limited type experience relevant to the in-flight emergency response.

Records could not establish whether recent maintenance was performed on the seat, suggesting a possible maintenance or inspection shortfall.
Banner tow operations during a low-altitude climb-out create high workload, which may have contributed to the pilot's inability to recover quickly from the disruption.

The oil sump valve (part of the engine oil system) was found closed and could be partially opened only by force, starving the engine of oil and causing rod separation, which points to an engine oil system component failure.

Connecting rods Nos. 1 through 4 were damaged and Nos. 1 and 2 separated from the crankshaft, indicating catastrophic engine internal (reciprocating engine) failure as the consequence of lubrication loss.
Maintenance records lack documentation of when the oil sump valve was installed and the oil change was skipped at the annual, suggesting maintenance/inspection deficiencies contributed.
The owner performed oil changes without tooling and the valve installer is unknown, pointing to maintenance task performance issues with the oil sump valve.

The descending left turn in a nose-down attitude at low altitude on base-to-final suggests a performance/control parameter exceedance such as an unrecovered stall or excessive descent during a low turn-to-final maneuver.
The flight instructor's belief that the pilot attempted a descending left 180° turn to runway 36 from the base leg indicates an inappropriate pilot action during the approach to landing.
Decision to attempt a steep descending turn back to a different runway at low altitude, rather than continuing the pattern, reflects a poor information processing or decision error.

A flight instructor and student crew on an instructional flight with student-pilot involvement suggests possible limited experience in the maneuver, though the packet provides no direct evidence of this.

Fuel-wetted debris obstructing the fuel shutoff valve inlet suggests a possible fuel flow restriction, but the engine ran normally and the cause of impact is unconfirmed, so this finding is weakly supported.
The No. 2 alternator belt broke, the sole charging source failed, and the electrical power system was lost, consistent with an electrical power system malfunction in the airplane.

The pilot did not correctly interpret or use the EFIS ammeter and battery alert information, continuing flight despite intermittent battery alerts, indicating improper use of available equipment and information.

The pilot had owned the homebuilt airplane for only about one month and may have lacked familiarity with its electrical system and alternator monitoring, which the builder described as relying on digital ammeters.
Maintenance and inspection practices on the alternator drive belt, which was last replaced in 2018 and not addressed in the 2023 annual, may have contributed to the belt failure.
Limited guidance from the builder on how to verify alternator function, including that indicator lights were not wired, may reflect inadequate training or information transfer.
The cause could not be determined from the evidence: airbrake position, anti-skid performance, and switch configuration remain unresolved after testing.

Crew information processing and decision-making, including failure to verify switch configuration (airbrake/ground switch and TR use) before landing, is a plausible contributing factor given undocumented cockpit switch positions.
Airbrake (flight control surface) deployment status could not be determined and ground spoilers/airbrakes not deployed would explain reduced deceleration, making the flight control system relevant.

Landing gear/brake system behavior (anti-skid and brake effectiveness problems with tire skid marks) is central to the runway overrun, but the wheel braking components tested without anomaly, so the gear system finding is uncertain.
Fuel system is not implicated in the packet; this code is weakly supported and should be omitted.
Engine misfire, backfiring and power loss shortly after takeoff, with corroded No. 3 cylinder spark plugs, point to an engine power loss from the engine itself.

The pilot took off without completing an engine run-up despite a reported engine burp during the prior flight, suggesting an information processing or decision error about the engine's airworthiness.
Fuel was left on the left tank with the boost pump on, and a fuel-related cause for the power reduction cannot be excluded, though the fuel system was found continuous and operational.
The last condition inspection and maintenance oversight may not have detected the corroded spark plugs, a possible maintenance-oversight contributor.
Substantial fuselage skin cracks at 45 degrees and a longitudinal crack aft of the wing, with disbonded strap at the splice, indicate a structural fuselage failure.
The general structures category covers the composite skin-splice construction and as-built deviations from the reference drawing that led to the failure.
As-built construction differed from the reference drawing (added plies, single strap butt joint instead of overlap), pointing to a manufacturing/production deviation.
Resin-filled gaps, voids, and disbonding at the composite splice point to a material/fluid bonding defect in the fuselage laminate construction.
No runway or surface involvement in this in-flight structural failure, so this code is unlikely to apply.

Wire strikes during low-altitude agricultural flight often result from perception difficulty of thin wires near the pilot's field of view, a possible perception/orientation factor.
The nose landing gear actuator ball screw assembly failed by buckling and overstress fracture, and the airplane veered on landing, pointing to a landing gear system failure.
The extension tube housing fractured and splayed outward from off-axis contact, indicating a structural component failure in the nose gear mounting area.

Configuring gear and flaps while handling traffic-pattern radio communications suggests a workload management problem during a critical phase of flight.

Engine fuel and control issues, including the misfiring on taxi, the partially closed carburetor heat door, and the carburetor bowl fuel condition, point to a carburetor-related power loss.

The pilot continued the takeoff in a swell and wake environment and did not correctly respond to repeated skipping, indicating an information processing or decision error in handling the takeoff.

The pilot's control action during the skipping sequence, such as failing to apply proper back pressure and power per the skipping recovery procedure, led to the sharp pitch-up and loss of control.

The pilot's decision to set up for an off-field landing rather than another option is a possible decision-related contributing factor, though the packet offers little evidence of a poor choice.

The air race context involved closely spaced racers in the traffic pattern with competitive pressure and no traffic separation service, which the packet suggests contributed to the close, tight downwind spacing.

Pilots judged and flew downwind and base positions differently from each other and from expectations (wider base, tighter downwind, closer-in downwind), indicating flawed information processing or decision making about relative traffic positions.

Position reporting by radio was congested with unintelligible transmissions and pilots relied on abeam and base calls without clear traffic separation, suggesting communication breakdown.

Maintenance and inspection of the fuel filter per the service manual intervals appears not to have been performed, a maintenance/inspection deficiency.
The cause of the power loss could not be determined from the post-accident examination, as the fuel system, engine compression, and magnetos all tested within normal limits.

Loss of power shortly after takeoff from water with no found mechanical fault suggests a fuel-related engine problem such as fuel delivery or fuel control, though the examination found fuel and pump function normal.
Pilot's decision to attempt takeoff or continue flight at treetop height after power loss may reflect information processing or decision-making issues, though the narrative does not establish this.
Loss of aileron roll control while pitch control remained normal indicates a flight control system malfunction, specifically the aileron cable and bellcrank system.

The aileron control failure with ailerons ineffective points to a wing/aileron control linkage problem, and the right aileron cable contact and wear fall within the wing structure area around the aileron bellcrank.
Routing of the ELT antenna cable between the aileron bellcrank and cover plate and cable wear suggest a maintenance or rigging deficiency that allowed interference with aileron movement.
The examination found no restriction of bellcrank movement during testing, so the precise cause of the aileron failure remains undetermined.

The power line obstacle, with a clearance of about 21.8 ft above the sunflower canopy and an airplane height of 13.75 ft, is an object in the physical environment that the airplane struck.
Planning of the low-altitude spray route under the power lines appears inadequate given the prior wire strike the week before, though this is inferred rather than documented.
Attention to the wire obstacle during low-level spraying may have lapsed, as the pilot continued flying under the lines, but this cannot be confirmed without the logbooks or recorder data.

The bent throttle control found in the full-throttle position and the manufacturer advisory on uncommanded high-speed ground acceleration point to an engine control/throttle problem.
The pilot's apparent start-up or throttle handling without intent to fly, combined with the advisory on starting procedure and throttle control, suggests an action error contributing to the event.
The advisory emphasizes ground operations, starting procedure and throttle control, implying improper use of equipment during start and taxi.
Water contamination and corrosion-related water in the fuel strainer, carburetor bowl and tanks caused fuel contamination leading to rough running and power loss.

Annual inspection and maintenance did not detect degraded fuel cap gaskets, tank corrosion, and water in tanks, and the service bulletin for additional drains was not applied.
Airplane was stored outside with rain showers in the two weeks before the accident, a environmental factor that allowed water ingress into the fuel tanks.
The landing gear main spring assembly separated during takeoff roll, causing the airplane to veer off the runway, so the landing gear system is the failed component.
Fatigue cracking from corrosion pits and questionable repair/refinishing of the spring, with corrosion under primer, points to inadequate maintenance and inspection of the gear spring.
The left main gear spring assembly fractured from the fuselage underside, a structural failure of the airframe attachment, though the taxonomy's structure codes map most closely to fuselage here.

The 2010 repair involving magnetic particle inspection, retempering and shot peening, and the apparent corrosion beneath primer suggest a maintenance task performance issue that was not caught in later inspections.
Oversight of the required inspection of the main gear springs for corrosion and cracks appears to have failed to detect the progressive fatigue cracking over many years.

The accident involved a retractable-gear Piper with landing gear cycling and an anomaly-linked electrical spike during the gear sequence, pointing to a landing gear system-related factor, though testing found no anomalies.
The packet states the reason for the sharp amperage increase during the landing roll could not be determined, so the cause remains undetermined.
The sharp amperage spikes recorded during gear operation and landing roll suggest an electrical power system anomaly as a possible contributor to the outboard right wing damage event.

The fly-by-wire flight control system's AOA limiter protection engaged and limited elevator response to pilot pitch commands, so the flight control system's behavior contributed to the inability to arrest the porpoise and touchdown.

The crew continued an approach with the AOA limiter engaged before flare and did not initiate a go-around, and the pilots' aggressive, oscillating sidestick inputs prolonged disengagement, reflecting information processing and decision issues.
A sudden wind gust increased the airplane's AOA and triggered the AOA limiter engagement during the approach, with gusting winds up to 23 kt present.
The crew was unaware the AOA limiter had engaged, and the copilot's reaction and pilot's aggressive inputs indicate attention/monitoring failures during the high-workload final approach.

The left wing separated in flight after its forward and aft spars showed overload fracture signatures at a previously repaired, spliced and sleeved spar, indicating wing structural failure.
Toxicology showed high methamphetamine and amphetamine levels plus THC and amitriptyline, which likely impaired the pilot's psychomotor performance and control inputs during the erratic maneuvering.
The pilot lacked a valid pilot certificate and logbooks could not establish flight experience, suggesting inadequate qualification for the maneuvers flown.
The pilot performed low-altitude practice maneuvers and a steep-banked turn that led to a nose-low attitude and overstress, suggesting poor decision making about flight loads.
Maintenance records were not located and the kit manufacturer would not approve a sleeve repair, indicating inadequate oversight of the spar repair.
The muffler's internal flame tube blocked at least 95% of the tailpipe exit, a degraded exhaust component failure directly matching the exhaust system engine-exhaust category.
The annual/100-hour inspection included the exhaust stacks scope item yet the muffler's internal blockage was not detected, indicating an inspection deficiency.

The muffler had been repaired with flame tubes and tailpipe replaced and the exhaust system was not overhauled per the 800-hour guidance, reflecting maintenance and inspection shortfalls for the exhaust system.
Maintenance guidance recommended removing and inspecting the muffler every 100 hours, but the mechanic's inspections did not address it, suggesting a training or oversight gap in inspection practice.

Rough running on mixture changes and high fuel flow of about 22 gph point to an engine fuel and control problem, such as the fuel metering or mixture setting after the recent fuel pump adjustment and overhaul.
A recent engine overhaul and fuel pump adjustment about 12 days before the accident suggest a possible maintenance task performance deficiency affecting fuel metering.
The packet does not establish a definitive cause; the post-accident engine test ran normally, so the root cause remains undetermined.
The instructor's response to the abnormal fuel flow and rough running, cycling the mixture, may reflect an info processing or decision issue in managing the engine anomaly.
The No. 4 cylinder exhaust valve and piston failures with separated valve stems and piston hole indicate an engine internal failure in the Rotax 915 engine.
The operator's failure to perform required 50-hour oil and leaded-fuel inspections and its inconsistent fuel blend measurement point to deficient maintenance policy and procedure.
The maintenance team's mistaken belief about the AVGAS blend ratio led to omitted required 50-hour oil system maintenance, a maintenance task performance error.
Lead and carbon residue on valves and excessive guide wear point to oil system and lubrication deficiencies in the engine.
Valve guide tolerances exceeding limits in the heavy maintenance inspection suggest the inspection process did not identify worn components before flight.

The pilots flew at night in IMC toward a convective weather area using non-certified internet radar imagery, suggesting poor information processing and decision-making about continuing into deteriorating weather.
Night instrument meteorological conditions with convective weather in the area reduced visibility and ceiling, creating an environmental condition central to the loss of control in this accident.
A convective SIGMET was moving across the route, so convective weather and associated severe turbulence were present in the operating area.

The pilot performed a low pass and then a climbing left turn shortly after recently replacing the propeller governor, suggesting a flight-decision or information-processing error during a low-altitude maneuver near terrain, though the cause of the loss of control is not determined.

Maintenance logbooks were not located and the engine was removed and reinstalled by an owner-builder with limited mechanic involvement, indicating a possible maintenance or inspection deficiency relevant to the governor installation.

Toxicology showed ethanol and diphenhydramine in the pilot, which could have impaired judgment during the low pass, though the levels are low and their causal role is uncertain.
The airport had no policy or procedure requiring NOTAMs or coordination for ground maintenance work such as mowing near an active runway, and the manager was unaware NOTAMs were needed.

Communication between the airport manager and the grounds worker about the mowing location and pilots' awareness of work in progress was absent, as the worker moved to the airport without direction and no NOTAM was issued.
The runway environment included an unexpected ground worker and mower adjacent to the runway edge, a physical workspace hazard on the operating surface margin contributing to the close encounter.
A crosswind caused the airplane to drift right of runway centerline during the flare, bringing the right wing toward the mower near the runway edge.

The packet does not describe the phase of flight, the events leading to the damage, or any system anomaly, and the post-accident engine, fuel, and magneto checks were normal, so the cause cannot be determined from the facts given.

Get-there-itis, social pressure to meet the girlfriend, and invested time suggest motivational and mental/emotional state factors that drove the decision to press on.
Night, haze from wildfire smoke, clouds obscuring lights, and transition into IMC over the lake created ceiling/visibility conditions that contributed to loss of control.

The pilot did not respond to repeated text warnings and did not divert, suggesting inadequate attention to or monitoring of weather and safety information.
